title: Word order: two simple rules
summary: The engine goes last, and anything that describes something goes before it. Particles do the rest of the work.

blocks.text: You will hear two claims about Japanese word order: "it is subject-object-verb" and "order does not matter". Both come from asking European questions about Japanese. Mary-hit-Susan can be メアリーがスーザンをなぐった or スーザンをメアリーがなぐった. Who did what to whom is decided by **が** and **を**, not by position. Yet order does matter in two other places.
Whatever the engine is (a verb, an い-adjective, or a noun plus だ / です), it closes the logical sentence. A few sentence-ending particles such as ね may follow, but the engine is the true end.
Rule 2: a describer goes before what it describes

Anything that modifies a thing (a noun) must stand in front of it: a blue dress, the dress I bought at the market. Japanese never wraps a clause on the other side, as English does with "the dress **I bought**". So you always read in the same direction.
Take a full clause and move one piece to the engine end: it stops being a sentence and becomes a describer for that piece.

cars.label: the dress I bought at the market

blocks.text: 市場で買ったドレス。 The dress (I) bought at the market.

How do you know whether something is a full sentence or a describer? Look at the end. If it ends in an engine, it is a logical clause. If it ends in a noun, that noun is the thing being described by everything in front of it.

blocks.jp: 市場で買ったドレスを友達にあげた。
blocks.en: (I) gave my friend the dress I bought at the market.

blocks.jp: ドレスを買った市場は駅の近くだ。
blocks.en: The market where (I) bought the dress is near the station.

blocks.jp: 赤い帽子をかぶっている少女が笑った。
blocks.en: The girl wearing a red hat laughed.

items: **Rule 1:** the engine (verb, adjective or noun + copula) goes at the end.
**Rule 2:** anything that modifies a noun goes before it.
**が** and **を** show who and what; position does not.
A clause that ends in a noun is a describer, not a sentence.

questions.instruction: Rule 1: where does the engine of a sentence go?
questions.note: The engine closes the logical sentence.

questions.instruction: Which word is the engine?
questions.prompt: 妹が公園で友達と遊んだ。
questions.note: The verb comes last and closes the sentence.
questions.en: My little sister played with a friend in the park.

questions.instruction: Who saw whom?
questions.note: が marks the carriage (the one who saw) and を the thing seen, wherever they stand.

questions.instruction: True or false: swapping the places of the が and を phrases changes who did what to whom.
questions.note: が and を decide the roles, not position.

questions.instruction: Which one is a describer, not a full sentence?
questions.note: It ends in a noun, so everything before 本 describes it.

questions.instruction: In this phrase, what is 友達?
questions.note: A phrase that ends in a noun describes that noun.
questions.en: the friend I met at the station

questions.instruction: Which sentence breaks Rule 1 (engine last)?
questions.note: In the third sentence the engine 見た is not last.

questions.instruction: Fill the gap
questions.prompt: 駅の近く＿＿ある店は安い。
questions.note: に marks where the shop is, and the whole phrase describes 店.
questions.en: The shop near the station is cheap.

questions.instruction: Which is the main engine of the whole sentence?
questions.prompt: 先生が買った本を学生が読んだ。
questions.note: 買った only describes 本; the sentence ends with 読んだ.
questions.en: The student read the book the teacher bought.

questions.instruction: Which piece is a full clause (it ends in an engine)?
questions.note: 友達に会った ends in a verb; the others end in a noun.

questions.instruction: True or false?
questions.prompt: 母が作った料理 describes 料理, the food that Mother made.
questions.note: Anything that modifies a noun goes before it.

questions.instruction: What decides who did what to whom?
questions.note: Particles carry the roles; position does not.

questions.instruction: True or false: in 青い大きな車, both 青い and 大きな describe 車.
questions.note: Both describers stand in front of the noun they describe.

questions.instruction: Which one is a describer, not a full sentence?
questions.note: 来た友達 ends in a noun.

questions.instruction: Tap the noun that the clause 妹が買った describes
questions.note: 妹が買った describes かばん, so it is the thing described.
questions.en: The bag my little sister bought is blue.

questions.instruction: Tap the engine of the whole sentence
questions.note: 駅で会った describes 友達; 笑った is the engine.
questions.en: The friend I met at the station laughed.

questions.instruction: Tap the word that 昨日読んだ describes
questions.note: A clause that ends in a verb goes before the noun it describes.
questions.en: (I) lent my friend the book I read yesterday.

questions.instruction: Tap the true engine (ね may follow it)
questions.note: です is the engine; ね is only a sentence-ending particle.

questions.instruction: Build the sentence
questions.prompt: I read the book I bought yesterday.
questions.note: The describer goes before 本, and the engine is last.
questions.en: I read the book I bought yesterday.

questions.instruction: Build the sentence
questions.prompt: I ate at the restaurant near the station.
questions.note: 駅の近くの describes レストラン; the engine closes the sentence.
questions.en: I ate at the restaurant near the station.

questions.instruction: Build the sentence
questions.prompt: The food my mother made is delicious.
questions.note: 母が作った is a clause that describes 料理.
questions.en: The food my mother made is delicious.

questions.instruction: Build the sentence
questions.prompt: A small dog is running in the park.
questions.note: The describer goes before 犬; the engine is last.
questions.en: A small dog is running in the park.
